subtopic: Online communities, echo chambers and moderation
passage:
“Bhai, everyone thinks the captain is useless,” Kunal said, phone in hand at the kitchen counter. “My whole feed says so.”
Lalit peered over. “Who's in your feed?”
“The same five accounts. And the fan pages.”
“Did you follow anyone who likes him?”
“Why would I? They'd be wrong.”
“Kunal, at the ground yesterday half the team was defending him.”
Kunal frowned. “Nobody said that online.”
“Because the feed shows you what you already like.”
Mummy called from the next room, “What are you two arguing about?”
“Cricket,” said Lalit.
After a moment, Kunal followed one account that disagreed, then quickly muted it.

qa.q: Who did Kunal say were in the feed?
qa.a: Kunal said the same five accounts and the fan pages were in the feed.

qa.q: What does Kunal think about the captain, and why does Kunal think so?
qa.a: Kunal thinks everyone agrees the captain is useless because the whole feed says so, and does not realise the feed only shows agreeing voices.

qa.q: What was the turning point at the end of the passage?
qa.a: Kunal followed one account that disagreed, which widens the picture a little, but then quickly muted it, so the change is not settled.

qa.q: What might Lalit have been thinking when Lalit said half the team was defending the captain?
qa.a: Lalit seems to want Kunal to see the real spread of opinions and probably wonders how narrow Kunal's view of the world has become.

grounding: A teenager follows only accounts that agree, thinks everyone thinks the same, and begins to doubt when an older sibling offers a different picture.

subtopic: Online communities, echo chambers and moderation
passage: I'm Devika, and last year I followed only accounts that loved one band. My feed told me the rival band was awful and that everyone knew it. I stopped watching videos from the other side and muted a friend who liked them. At lunch in the school canteen I said, loudly, “Nobody serious likes their music.” Tarun, from my class, looked up. “Half of Class 10 does, Devika. I do.” Two other classmates at the table nodded. I sat there with my sandwich, realising that the picture I'd built was a lot narrower than the room I was sitting in. It was an odd feeling, like finding a wall in what I'd thought was open space.

qa.q: What did Devika say loudly at lunch in the canteen?
qa.a: Devika said, “Nobody serious likes their music.”

qa.q: Why did Devika think everyone agreed about the rival band?
qa.a: Devika followed only accounts that loved one band, so the feed kept showing agreement, and the picture of everyone felt complete.

qa.q: What could Devika do after the canteen moment?
qa.a: Devika could follow a few accounts that like the other band, listen to a song from it and ask Tarun what people like about it.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt when Tarun said, “Half of Class 10 does, Devika. I do”?
qa.a: Tarun may have felt a little defensive and a little brave about admitting to the liking in front of the table, and probably was glad that two others nodded.

grounding: A teenager follows only accounts that agree and begins to think everyone thinks the same, until someone in the class shows a wider picture.

subtopic: Online communities, echo chambers and moderation
passage: When Osaka's schools announced a phone ban, Yuki started following accounts that called it ridiculous. The more she liked, the more the feed showed her: memes, angry teachers from other cities, students swearing they'd protest. After three weeks she was sure every teenager in the country agreed with her. In the class debate, Dalia, the exchange student from Madrid, stood up and said she actually liked the ban; she slept better and talked more at lunch. Half the class nodded. Yuki's face went hot. 'But everyone thinks it's stupid,' she said. The teacher asked, 'Everyone where?' Yuki opened her mouth, then closed it. That evening she scrolled her feed and realised she hadn't seen a single post from the other side.

qa.q: Where was Dalia an exchange student from?
qa.a: Madrid.

qa.q: How did Yuki feel when half the class nodded at Dalia?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and shocked, her face hot, because she had believed everyone agreed with her.

qa.q: What could Yuki try to widen her picture?
qa.a: Follow a few thoughtful accounts from the other side and talk to classmates like Dalia before deciding what 'everyone' thinks.

qa.q: What might it be like for Dalia to speak up for the ban?
qa.a: Probably a little nervous as an exchange student going against a loud opinion, and reassured when half the class nodded.

grounding: A teenager's feed shows only agreement until she believes everyone thinks the same, and a class debate reveals the narrowing.

subtopic: Online communities, echo chambers and moderation
passage: At the school football club meeting, the coach asked what everyone thought of Sunday's final. Mohit jumped in. 'The referee was paid off. Everyone knows.' He'd spent the weekend on a fan page where thousands of posts said so; the more he liked them, the more appeared, each angrier than the last. Dilnaz, the team's goalkeeper, frowned. 'I watched the replay. That penalty was fair.' Two others agreed. Mohit stared. On his screen, nobody thought that. The coach put the replay on the club laptop, and they watched it together in slow motion. Mohit went quiet. 'My feed only showed the other angle,' he mumbled. Dilnaz shrugged. 'Feeds show what you like, not what happened.'

qa.q: Where did the coach show the replay?
qa.a: On the club laptop.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when Dilnaz said the penalty was fair?
qa.a: He felt surprised and confused, since on his screen nobody thought that.

qa.q: What did the coach do that helped, and what could Mohit do next time?
qa.a: Showed the replay so everyone checked the facts together; next time Mohit could look at a clip or ask others before trusting a feed that only agrees with him.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz see Mohit's claim?
qa.a: Having watched the replay, Dilnaz likely found it frustrating and a bit funny, and pointed out that feeds show what you like, not what happened.

grounding: A teenager's feed rewards one angry view until he believes everyone agrees, and the team's replay shows the narrowing.

subtopic: Online communities, echo chambers and moderation
passage:
Dear Jomon chetta,
Something weird happened, and you're the only one who won't laugh. For two months I followed only pages that post about how parents ruin everything: screenshots of strict rules, memes about old-fashioned uncles. I liked them all, and my feed filled up with nothing else. I started thinking every parent in the world was the enemy, even Amma.
Then on Sunday, Amma sat up with me till two, helping me finish my model after I panicked. And I thought, wait, none of my pages would ever post this.
I scrolled back and saw I hadn't seen a single nice parent story in weeks. Not because they don't exist. Because I never clicked on them.
I've started unfollowing some pages. It feels strange, and a bit lonely.
Disha

qa.q: Until what time did Amma help Disha on Sunday?
qa.a: Till two.

qa.q: How does Disha feel after unfollowing some pages?
qa.a: Disha feels strange and a bit lonely, since the feed had become familiar company.

qa.q: What else could Disha do to keep a wider picture?
qa.a: Follow a few accounts with different views and talk about real moments, like Amma's help, with friends offline.

qa.q: How might Amma feel if she read the letter?
qa.a: She would likely be touched that her help changed Disha's view, and relieved not to be seen as the enemy.

grounding: A teenager realises her feed showed only one kind of post until she believed everyone thought the same.

subtopic: Online communities, echo chambers and moderation
passage: Naveen, you asked why I got so heated at the debate. Okay, the honest version from me, Tenzin. It started with one video about the city cutting trees for the flyover. I liked it. The next day my feed gave me ten more. Then only those. Every account I followed said the same thing, louder. After a month I genuinely believed every sane person in Shillong agreed with me. So in the school debate, when Dolkar said the flyover would cut her mum's commute by an hour, I laughed. Like, who even thinks that? And half the hall went quiet. That's when I saw it. I hadn't heard a single other view in weeks. Not because there weren't any. My feed had just stopped showing them. I've followed two people who disagree now. It's annoying. It's probably good for me.

qa.q: What was the first video about?
qa.a: It was about the city cutting trees for the flyover.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when half the hall went quiet?
qa.a: Tenzin felt embarrassed and shaken, suddenly seeing that no other view had come through in weeks.

qa.q: What small step did Tenzin take to widen the feed, and why does it help?
qa.a: Following two people who disagree lets other views back in, so the picture of the world stops shrinking without notice.

qa.q: How might Dolkar have felt when Tenzin laughed?
qa.a: Dolkar probably felt dismissed and hurt, since a real reason about her mum's commute was treated as foolish.

grounding: Tenzin describes how a feed that showed only agreeing accounts narrowed the picture of the world until a debate exposed it.
